newsitem.title: CHILE: Americas trade talks are bound to be tense - Daley.
newsitem.headline: Americas trade talks are bound to be tense - Daley.

text.p: Tensions at a meeting of Western Hemisphere trade ministers in Brazil last week may forshadow even tougher confrontations during negotiation of regional free trade pact next year, U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley said on Monday.

Daley, in Chile for a three-day visit, said tensions between the United States and the four-nation Mercosur group at the meeting in Belo Horizonte was a natural and unavoidable feature of any big multilateral trade meeting.
But even sharper tensions will probably await negotiators as they start the task of trying to hammer out a free trade agreement for the whole Western Hemisphere starting in March 1998, he said.
"Whenever you get that many trade ministers together at one time, you're definitely going to have some tension," Daley told a news conference after meeting Chilean President Eduardo Frei.

At the Belo Horizonte meeting, Brazil and the other Mercosur nations -- Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay -- chafed at U.S. calls for a quick start and an all-inclusive agenda in the negotiation of a Free Trade Area of the Americas, which Washington hopes to establish by 2005.
In the end, both sides agreed to start formal talks after a hemispheric summit in Chile next March, but with gaping holes over the scope of the negotiations left to be resolved later.

Daley also said the Clinton administration might be willing to drop its insistence on labour and environmental provisions to fast-track trade legislation to win approval for the bill in the U.S. Congress.
The White House bill "may or may not include labour and environmental standards" when it's proposed, he said. "No decision has been made on what the bill will look like."

Fast-track legislation has been deadlocked in Congress over the Republican majority's refusal to allow labour and environmental standards to be included in the agenda of future trade talks. President Bill Clinton, under pressure from within his own Democratic Party, has until now insisted that those issues be included.
The lack of fast-track has held up U.S. trade negotiations on various fronts, including with Chile which is next in line to join the North American Free Trade Agreement.

Daley said earlier the White House was counting on getting fast-track passed in time for the Chile summit, which the leaders of every country in the Americas are due to attend, except Cuba's Fidel Castro.
